short.en: How many ways can a sentence be read?

t.en: “Old men and women”: are the women old too, or only the men? The same words, merged into phrases two at a time in different ways, mean different things: (old men) and women, or old (men and women). Draw the merging out and you get a parse tree.

Suppose any two neighbouring stretches of words can be merged. How many different ways are there to merge a run of words? An interval table again: cell (i, j) records “how many ways words i to j can be merged”. A single word has just 1, so the diagonal is already filled in.

The last merge joins a left stretch and a right stretch. At a given split point, the left side has some number of ways and the right side some number, and any left way can go with any right way: how many ways does this split point give? And how should the different split points be combined?

When merging stones, each split point was “left + right”, and you picked the cheapest. What about here? Broom’s sweep arm sends the left parts and right parts by split point as before, and a Multiplier can multiply them pair by pair too.

goal.en: A run of words is merged two at a time into phrases until it becomes one whole sentence. Work out how many different ways of merging there are (how many parse trees).

how.en: The sweep arm sends the left part and right part for every split point.

body.en: 3 words, 2 ways; 4 words, 5; 5 words, 14: these are the Catalan numbers, and they grow very fast as words are added. That is why a computer analysing a sentence doesn’t list every tree, but works through this interval table cell by cell.
Real parsing (the CKY algorithm) also checks grammar rules: which two stretches can merge, and into what. The table has exactly the same shape.

note.en: Parse trees: “left × right” at each split point, then add them up.

hints.en: Look at a single split point first: every way on the left can go with every way on the right. How many is that in all?
Every split point’s result counts: wire them into “sum”.
